genres.claim: A source on a modern whodunit says the form wants heightened, larger-than-life suspects who still read as real people; nothing found supports a distinct technique for withholding secrets.
genres.source: SlashFilm, ''Knives Out' Director Rian Johnson And Star Michael Shannon On Blending Comedy With Mystery...', https://www.slashfilm.com/570824/knives-out-interview/
genres.sourceSupports: Johnson: "you need to get great actors and actors who can do performances that are this big but still feel like real people." He also says "all of the funniest lines in the movie, Michael just shouted out on the day." A separate search snippet (Screen Rant, not opened) says Johnson gives actors the full script including the killer's identity.
genres.uncertainty: One director on one comic whodunit. Nothing found says what mystery asks of actors generally; 'withholding and layering' remains the researcher's reading. Shannon's ad-libs do not establish improvisation as a convention of the form.

genres.claim: Noir, which neo-noir revives, is defined partly by first-person voice-over narration, so a lead may carry a narrating voice track; a secondary source describes its delivery as deadpan.
genres.source: Dartmouth Library, 'Film noir' research guide, quoting Kuhn & Westwell, A Dictionary of Film Studies (Oxford, 2020), https://researchguides.dartmouth.edu/filmgenres/noir; secondary: Voquent, 'Voice Over in Film Noir', https://www.voquent.com/blog/voice-over-in-film-noir/ (403; snippet only)
genres.sourceSupports: Oxford definition (via the guide) lists "dreamlike first-person voice-over narration" among noir's narrative strategies. Voquent snippet: the detective's internal monologue is "delivered in a deadpan manner." The guide says nothing about acting style.

tags.why: The Oxford definition names first-person voice-over narration as a noir convention; this is about classic noir, and its carry-over to neo-noir is inferred from neo-noir's definition as a revival of noir tropes.

genres.uncertainty: No source about neo-noir acting specifically was found. 'Cool understatement' and 'controlled menace' are unsupported. Many neo-noirs drop the voice-over.

genres.claim: The best-known Nordic noir lead describes a performance built from tight control of a closed, socially difficult character; the genre is characterised as slow and melancholic, but nothing found ties a specific acting style to the genre.
genres.source: Barry Forshaw, 'SOFIA ON SAGA: Sofia Helin talks Saga Norén and The Bridge', Crime Time, https://www.crimetime.co.uk/sofia-on-saga-sofia-helin-talks-saga-noren-and-the-bridge-to-barry-forshaw/
genres.sourceSupports: Helin: "At first I regarded her as a blank wall, but then that blank wall became a glass wall and I was able to see through it"; she chose to make it look like Saga "was forcing herself to do eye contact"; "I usually have to keep Saga within certain parameters." Search snippets (genre sites, not opened) describe Nordic noir's "slow and melancholic pace".
genres.uncertainty: One character in one series; Saga's restraint is a character trait, not evidence of a genre-wide style. No scholarly source on Nordic noir performance was found. Bilingual productions (The Bridge) suggest language demands but no source said so.

genres.claim: Possession scenes in occult horror have demanded extreme vocal and physical-makeup work, as in The Exorcist, where the demon's voice was a separate, punishing vocal performance and the possessed actor wore long-applied prosthetics.
genres.source: Jacob Slankard, 'The Actor Behind the Demon's Voice in The Exorcist Went to Hell and Back', Collider, https://collider.com/the-exorcist-demon-voice-mercedes-mccambridge/
genres.sourceSupports: Mercedes McCambridge "insisted on being tightly bound to a chair, swallowing raw eggs and Jack Daniel's while smoking" to get "a wheezing, roughshod quality"; lines were recorded multiple times with separate "laughs, cries, and other animal noises" added; Blair "couldn't supply a suitable voice". Search snippets (Looper, not opened) say Linda Blair spent two to five hours a day in makeup and was harnessed for the thrashing scenes.

tags.why: Collider documents the demon as a voice-only performance by a separate actor, built from extreme vocal technique.
Only the Looper snippet (not opened) supports the multi-hour prosthetic makeup for the possessed character.

genres.uncertainty: A single film; whether possession scenes generally use these methods is not established. The prosthetic detail is snippet-only. 'Sustained dread and belief in unseen forces' is unsupported.

genres.claim: Screen parody of the Airplane! school asks actors to deliver absurd material with complete dramatic seriousness, deadpan, oblivious to the gags around them.
genres.source: 'R.I.P. Leslie Nielsen', The A.V. Club, https://www.avclub.com/r-i-p-leslie-nielsen-1798223005
genres.sourceSupports: Nielsen could invest "the most ridiculous lines of dialogue with a delivery that was serious as a heart attack"; the Zucker-Abrahams-Zucker team cast him as "an archetypal straight man oblivious to the constant stream of gags going on around him." Search snippet of Nielsen's 1993 Fresh Air interview (NPR; timed out on fetch): approaching the material "with the same seriousness and the same gravity" as their police shows "would be very funny."

tags.why: The A.V. Club credits the comedy to Nielsen's deadpan delivery of ridiculous lines, i.e. verbal comic timing played straight.

genres.uncertainty: One school of parody (ZAZ). Parody that relies on mimicry of a specific performer (sketch parody) was not researched. 'Precise imitation of a recognisable style' is not directly supported.

genres.claim: The model screen picaresque was carried by its lead's charm across an episodic, roistering narrative; nothing found generalises this into a performance demand.
genres.source: Criterion Collection, 'Tom Jones (1963)', https://www.criterion.com/films/28736-tom-jones (403 on fetch; seen via search snippet)
genres.sourceSupports: Search snippet: Tom Jones is "a spirited picaresque"; "Albert Finney gives a career-defining performance as the foundling whose easy charm seems to lead him astray at every turn." Another snippet (source unclear) mentions "asides to the screen."
genres.uncertainty: One film, snippet only. No source on what picaresque asks of actors generally. 'Shifting register across settings' is unsupported. The 'asides to the screen' line could not be attributed and was not used for a tag.

genres.claim: Police procedurals train their casts in real procedure (classroom instruction, traffic stops, cuffing, clearing a house, defensive tactics, ride-alongs) so the actions read as second nature on camera.
genres.source: Michael Cudlitz, 'Ride-Along (I'm Not a Cop, But I Look Like One on TV)', HuffPost, https://www.huffpost.com/entry/southland-preview_b_1211491
genres.sourceSupports: Cudlitz (who played John Cooper on Southland): "We started in a classroom covering many of the things we would be required to do on film as cops"; training covered car positioning at traffic stops, cuffing, clearing a house and defensive tactics, ending in a ride-along with an on-duty officer; the aim was for procedure to become "second nature."
genres.uncertainty: One show, written by its actor. Defensive tactics are mentioned but not as sustained fight work, so stunt is not applied. 'Restraint in interrogation' is unsupported. No tag in the vocabulary covers procedural fluency.

genres.claim: Political drama in the Sorkin mould asks actors to master fast, dense, exact dialogue through heavy repetition so it becomes subconscious, often delivered on the move.
genres.source: Screen Rant, 'The West Wing's Bradley Whitford Explains Aaron Sorkin's Speedy Dialogue', https://screenrant.com/bradley-whitford-west-wing-aaron-sorkin-dialogue/
genres.sourceSupports: Whitford: actors must "learn your lines as fast as you can" and do "endless repetitions" to make dialogue "subconscious, so that technical aspect of the performance was removed"; Sorkin writes "racing, like, just ahead of the audience." Search snippet (Cheat Sheet, not opened): Martin Sheen said actors could suggest but not improvise, and Sorkin wanted lines verbatim because he wrote 'in meter'.
genres.uncertainty: This is one writer's style on one show, not the genre. Heightened was considered (the 'meter' claim) but that is snippet-only and writer-specific, so it is not applied. 'Quiet calculation of characters wielding power' is unsupported.

genres.claim: A leading conspiracy-thriller performance was built on stillness and near-invisibility rather than display; nothing found makes this a stated genre convention.
genres.source: The Film Stage, 'Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy Star Gary Oldman Talks His Subtle Performance...', https://thefilmstage.com/interview-tinker-tailor-soldier-spy-star-gary-oldman-talks-his-subtle-performance-james-bond-more/
genres.sourceSupports: Oldman cites le Carré's description of Smiley as a "swift" that can regulate its temperature to the room, "Almost like a chameleon", and says that passage "was where the stillness comes from"; he and Tomas Alfredson avoided details that would make Smiley memorable.
genres.uncertainty: Tinker Tailor is usually classed as a spy thriller, so it is an adjacent example, not a clean political-thriller one. Oldman does not use the words paranoia or restraint. No genre-level source found.

genres.claim: Post-apocalyptic leads have required extended fight training and drastic weight loss to look survival-worn.
genres.source: Collider, 'Tom Hardy Interview MAD MAX: FURY ROAD; Training, His Look...', https://collider.com/tom-hardy-interview-mad-max-fury-road-training-look-shooting-schedule-filming-george-miller/
genres.sourceSupports: Hardy: "I'll probably get three or four months of fight training out there. Seven days a week"; "I'm meant to drop 30 pounds"; "Imagine a hungry wolf." Search snippets (Spokesman-Review, Today, not opened) say Viggo Mortensen lost about 20-30 pounds for The Road.

tags.why: Hardy describes three to four months of daily fight training for the role.
Hardy's planned 30-pound loss (read directly) and Mortensen's weight loss (snippet) are physical transformations for the look of the role.

genres.uncertainty: Two films; Fury Road is as much an action film as a post-apocalyptic one. The 'little dialogue / silent movie' claim appeared only in an unverified snippet and was not confirmed by the Collider page read.

genres.claim: Some prison films build performance from authenticity: casting formerly incarcerated people and shooting improvised, documentary-feel ensemble scenes, or shooting in real former prisons.
genres.source: ABC News (Australia), 'Sing Sing tells a remarkable true story of a prison theatre program, starring Colman Domingo' (14 Jan 2025), https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-01-14/sing-sing-colman-domingo-interview/104791974
genres.sourceSupports: "More than 85 per cent of Sing Sing's cast is made up of formerly incarcerated men playing versions of themselves"; rehearsal scenes were "largely improvised and shot via Steadicam, giving them a documentary feel"; the directors "merely provided prompts." Search snippets say Starred Up was shot in a former Belfast prison with ex-convicts.
genres.uncertainty: Sing Sing's method is unusual, so improvisation is not a convention of the genre and is not tagged. 'Psychological toll of long confinement' is unsupported. No genre-level source found.

genres.claim: A central psychological-horror performance was played as grief and family drama pushed to extremes, with the horror grounded in something real rather than played as spectacle.
genres.source: Time, 'Toni Collette Interview on New Horror Hit Hereditary', https://time.com/5295637/toni-collette-hereditary-horror-interview/
genres.sourceSupports: Collette: the film is "a meditation on grief and people dealing with emotional pain"; on intense scenes, "trying to push it away from me until it was the moment between 'action' and 'cut'—resisting it and just letting it out at the right time"; she calls it and The Sixth Sense "not solely horror films."
genres.uncertainty: One film. Nothing found states 'subtlety and ambiguity rather than spectacle' as a genre demand; Collette's performance is in fact very large in places. No tag in the vocabulary fits.

genres.claim: Psychological thriller leads are often unreliable or self-concealing characters, and one leading example describes playing such a character as clinical and fully worked out in advance.
genres.source: Deadline, ''Gone Girl's Rosamund Pike: Portraying The Complicated Amazing Amy' (Dec 2014), https://deadline.com/2014/12/rosamund-pike-interview-gone-girl-oscars-1201332014/ (paywalled; seen via search snippet)
genres.sourceSupports: Search snippet: Pike says Amy is "not someone overpowered by rage but driven by rage"; playing her is not about unleashing something animal, everything is "worked out in advance," making her "so clinical that it gives the actress a buffer." A separate snippet of NPR Fresh Air (Natalie Portman on Black Swan) says she trained with New York City Ballet members.
genres.uncertainty: Snippet only; the page was not read. Single examples. Ballet in Black Swan is film-specific and does not support a dance tag for the genre.

genres.claim: Queer cinema is defined by its subjects, not by a performance technique; the only performer-side source found concerns intimacy coordination on queer productions.
genres.source: PinkNews, 'Intimacy co-ordinator behind major queer sex scenes reveals what their job is really like' (30 Oct 2024), https://www.thepinknews.com/2024/10/30/queer-intimacy-coordinator-robbie-taylor-hunt-mr-loverman-reverberation/
genres.sourceSupports: Robbie Taylor Hunt: before rehearsal he asks actors individually "This is what's in the script, what are we thinking about it? What do we want, and not want, to do?"; his work covers "simulated sex, nudity, kissing, physical touch..." and aims at the scene's intended emotional and narrative effect.
genres.uncertainty: Intimacy coordination is general industry practice, not specific to queer cinema, and not every queer film has intimate scenes, so intimacy is not tagged. 'Truthful, unstereotyped portrayal' is unsupported by any source read.

genres.claim: Revenge action films have required their leads to undergo months of full-time martial-arts and weapons training to carry the fight work.
genres.source: Collider, ''Kill Bill' Star... Reveals the Grueling Training Sessions', https://collider.com/uma-thurman-kill-bill-training-comments/
genres.sourceSupports: Thurman trained "three solid months, five days a week, nine to five", learning "knife-throwing, a little bit of target practice. Everything from fencing to samurai style, to Wushu style." Search snippets (Maxim, not opened) say Keanu Reeves trained eight hours a day for six months for John Wick.

tags.why: Thurman describes months of full-time fight and weapons training for the revenge story's fight sequences.

genres.uncertainty: Revenge dramas without action (e.g. slow-burn thrillers) exist and would not need this. 'Grief turning into obsession' is unsupported.

genres.claim: The road movie's in-car filming foregrounds dialogue between side-by-side travellers.
genres.source: Kuhn, A. & Westwell, G., 'Road movie', A Dictionary of Film Studies (Oxford University Press, 2020), as quoted on Dartmouth Library's 'Road films' research guide, https://researchguides.dartmouth.edu/filmgenres/roadfilms
genres.sourceSupports: "The physical constraints of filming in a car tend to lead to a heavy reliance on side-by-side shots and the foregrounding of dialogue"; road movies also favour "montage sequences, travelling and aerial shots, and diegetic music."
genres.uncertainty: The Oxford text was read as quoted by the Dartmouth guide, not in the original. It describes the form's shooting and dialogue, not what it asks of actors; 'gradual character change' is a narrative feature, not a performance demand. No vocabulary tag fits.

genres.claim: A rockumentary is a documentary about rock musicians, so its subjects are real performers; where actors are involved, the touchstone is the fictional mock-rockumentary, made with improvised dialogue by actor-musicians.
genres.source: BFI, 'Rob Reiner: how we made This Is Spinal Tap', https://www.bfi.org.uk/interviews/rob-reiner-how-we-made-this-spinal-tap; definition: Merriam-Webster 'rockumentary' (403; snippet only), https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/rockumentary
genres.sourceSupports: Reiner: "The entire film was improvised. The only speech that's not improvised is Patrick Macnee"; dialogue "was completely improvised." Search snippets (not the BFI page) say Guest, McKean and Shearer played their own instruments and performed the songs. Definition snippet: a documentary about rock music or its musicians.

tags.why: Reiner says This Is Spinal Tap's dialogue was entirely improvised; this applies to the mock form, not to real rockumentaries.
Snippet-only: the Spinal Tap actors performed the songs themselves; real rockumentaries feature musicians performing, per the definition snippet.

genres.uncertainty: For a true rockumentary there is no acted performance, so any actor demand comes from the mockumentary variant. The song tag rests on a snippet. The BFI page read does not mention the instruments.

genres.claim: Romance depends on believable chemistry between the leads, which casting tests with paired chemistry reads; nothing authoritative was read.
genres.source: Search snippets only (dictionary-style definition of 'chemistry read', source page not identified); 'Romantic Comedy Acting: Chemistry and Timing', The Playground, https://theplayground.com/romantic-comedy-acting-chemistry-and-timing/ (not opened)
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: a chemistry read is "an occasion when actors who are being considered for particular parts... read some of the script together, to see if they work well together and seem to have chemistry." Snippet claim that 'over seventy percent of romantic comedy casting decisions are based on chemistry reads' is unsourced and was not used.
genres.uncertainty: No credible source read. Intimacy was considered: SAG-AFTRA's intimacy-coordinator standards (seen only via snippets; PDF returned 403) cover nudity and simulated sex in any genre, not romance as such, so intimacy is not tagged.

genres.claim: A landmark romantic-drama lead described the role as unusually internal, requiring a mature, contained performance of longing; nothing found generalises this.
genres.source: PopEntertainment.com, Heath Ledger interview about Brokeback Mountain, http://www.popentertainment.com/ledger.htm (connection failed; seen via search snippet)
genres.sourceSupports: Search snippet: Ledger called Ennis "the most complex and internal character" he had been offered and said it would require "a more matured performance."
genres.uncertainty: Snippet only, one film. A snippet claiming Before Sunrise's dialogue was largely improvised was not used: it is unattributed and conflicts with the film being scripted. 'Heightened, sustained emotion... culminating in loss' is unsupported.

genres.claim: The defining screen satire Dr. Strangelove was built on one actor playing several caricatures, each found through voice and walk, and on largely improvised dialogue from characters unaware of their own absurdity.
genres.source: Far Out Magazine, 'Peter Sellers' defining performance in Dr Strangelove', https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/peter-sellers-stanley-kubrick-dr-strangelove/
genres.sourceSupports: Sellers played "US President Merkin Muffley, Dr. Strangelove and Captain Lionel Mandrake of the RAF"; Sellers: "I start with the voice... It's through the way he speaks that I find out the rest about him", then "how the character walks"; "Playing characters who are entirely unaware of just how absurd they are, Sellers improvised a majority of his dialogue, with Kubrick incorporating his ad-libs."

tags.why: Sellers built three distinct caricatures from voice and walk in one film, character work the source describes directly.
The source says Sellers improvised most of his dialogue and Kubrick kept the ad-libs; this is one film, not shown to be a convention of satire.

genres.uncertainty: Single film and a magazine source. The 'playing it with a straight face' idea is supported only by 'characters entirely unaware of how absurd they are'. Accent is not tagged because the source does not say accents were required, though the roles imply them.

genres.claim: No source found on what science fantasy specifically asks of an actor. The nearest material is an actor's account of effects-driven science-fiction work in general.
genres.source: Stephen Lang interview, Smashing Interviews Magazine, https://smashinginterviews.com/interviews/actors/stephen-lang-interview-avatar-star-on-his-current-role-in-the-fox-sci-fi-series-terra-nova ; genre definition pointer: Wikipedia, Science fantasy (pointer only)
genres.sourceSupports: Lang says green screen 'you really have to use your imagination' and demands specificity because you are 'seeing things that are going to be put there later'. Nothing in it is specific to science fantasy as opposed to science fiction.
genres.uncertainty: No genre-specific source. Green-screen imagination work has no tag in the fixed vocabulary. The earlier claim of 'stylised or physical action' is unsourced and was not carried over into tags.

genres.claim: Effects-heavy science fiction asks the actor to play against things that are not there, which takes imagination and specificity.
genres.source: Stephen Lang interview, Smashing Interviews Magazine, https://smashinginterviews.com/interviews/actors/stephen-lang-interview-avatar-star-on-his-current-role-in-the-fox-sci-fi-series-terra-nova
genres.sourceSupports: Lang (Avatar, Terra Nova) says green screen 'presents its own challenge', 'you really have to use your imagination', and you are 'seeing things that are going to be put there later'.
genres.uncertainty: One actor, read via snippet. It speaks to effects-driven production, not to science fiction as a genre (much science fiction has no green screen). The vocabulary has no tag for effects or green-screen work; 'camera' does not mean that, so no tag was given. Nothing found on technical exposition.

genres.claim: The slapstick comic must be acrobat and stunt performer as well as comedian, with perfect timing.
genres.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Slapstick', https://www.britannica.com/art/slapstick-comedy
genres.sourceSupports: Quoted in search results as: 'The slapstick comic, more than a mere funnyman or buffoon, must often be an acrobat, a stunt performer, and something of a magician—a master of uninhibited action and perfect timing.' The definition also names broad physical action and roots in commedia dell'arte.

tags.why: Britannica defines slapstick as comedy of broad physical action; the comic is 'a master of uninhibited action'.
Britannica says the slapstick comic 'must often be an acrobat, a stunt performer'.
Britannica names 'perfect timing' as part of the slapstick comic's mastery.

genres.uncertainty: Britannica returned HTTP 403 to a direct fetch; the quotation was returned verbatim by two separate searches but not read on the page. A Scribd copy of the Britannica article also appears in results.

genres.claim: Slasher leads, especially the final girl, do physical fight and stunt work in the climactic confrontation, often trained for it, alongside sustained fear.
genres.source: Fangoria, 'Q&A: Taissa Farmiga Talks The Standout Satirical Slasher THE FINAL GIRLS', https://www.fangoria.com/taissa-farmiga-the-final-girls-interview/ ; also BuzzFeed, 'The Last Final Girl: How Danielle Harris Survived...', https://www.buzzfeed.com/louispeitzman/from-child-actor-to-scream-queen-how-danielle-harris-became
genres.sourceSupports: Farmiga: 'I trained for the machete work in the fight scenes, and they had me practice a few times in the harness that would yank me backwards'; filming involved 'a lot of night work and being scared'. Harris (snippet): it was 'exhausting fighting these giant guys and kind of having to carry the movie physically as well as emotionally, because the Final Girl has to do both of those things.'

tags.why: Farmiga trained for machete fight work and harness pulls; Harris describes fighting stunt performers as a requirement of the final-girl role.

genres.uncertainty: Farmiga read directly; Harris only via snippet. Both speak about the final-girl lead, not every slasher role. Screaming is described (scream queen) but has no vocabulary tag. The Final Girls is a satirical slasher.

genres.claim: Slice of life depicts everyday experience in a naturalistic manner, often without conventional plot or climax.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Slice of life', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slice_of_life (pointer only); Harvard Film Archive, 'Ozu 120', https://harvardfilmarchive.org/programs/the-complete-yasujiro-ozu
genres.sourceSupports: Wikipedia: slice of life 'refers to a storytelling style that depicts everyday experiences in a naturalistic manner'. Harvard Film Archive (snippet) describes Ozu's films as exchanging ideas 'through gestures, glances, and plain assertions'.

tags.why: The cited definition makes naturalistic depiction of everyday life the genre's defining trait; this is the definition entailing the tag, not an acting source.

genres.uncertainty: Wikipedia is a pointer, and its definition is about storytelling, not acting. No acting source found. The camera tag rests on the definition only.

genres.claim: Space opera takes its name from the melodrama of opera, and Star Wars' dialogue was deliberately written in an old-fashioned, melodramatic serial style that actors found hard to speak.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Space opera', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_opera (pointer); FandomWire, 'Most people don't understand the style of Star Wars', https://fandomwire.com/most-people-dont-understand-the-style-of-star-wars-george-lucas-never-understood-a-star-wars-criticism-fueled-by-harrison-ford/
genres.sourceSupports: Wikipedia: the term refers to 'the melodrama, scope, and formulaic stories of operas'. FandomWire (snippet) quotes Lucas: the style is 'very much like a 1930s Western or Saturday matinee serial' and the dialogue was meant to represent filmmaking with 'a lot more melodrama'; Ford's line 'you can type this, but you can't say it' is widely quoted.

tags.why: Lucas, as quoted, says Star Wars dialogue was deliberately stylised in a 1930s melodramatic serial register, which is stylised language.

genres.uncertainty: The Lucas quote reaches me through a fan site; one franchise stands for the genre. Wikipedia's 'melodrama' is about story, not acting. Action and effects work were not sourced.

genres.claim: Leone's spaghetti westerns hold the actor's face in extreme close-up with little dialogue; Eastwood played the lead with an economy of words.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Sergio Leone', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_Leone (pointer); Remind Magazine, 'How Did Clint Eastwood Rise to Fame as a Spaghetti Western Antihero?', https://www.remindmagazine.com/article/41352/clint-eastwood-spaghetti-western-antihero-sergio-leone-dollars-trilogy/
genres.sourceSupports: Wikipedia (snippet): Leone's style juxtaposes extreme close-ups with long shots; he 'had a fascination with faces and used little dialogue'. Remind (snippet): Eastwood wanted to play the Man With No Name 'with an economy of words' and felt 'the less he said, the stronger he became'.

tags.why: The form's signature is the extreme close-up on a near-silent face, which asks for restrained on-camera playing; Eastwood's stated choice was minimal speech.

genres.uncertainty: Leone stands for the genre. Remind is a popular magazine. Neither source discusses gun or horse handling, which this genre likely shares with the Western.

genres.claim: No source found on what splatter asks of the actor specifically. Sources describe effects work and blood rigs rather than performance.
genres.source: Chicago Reader, 'Behind the gory scenes of Splatter Theater', https://chicagoreader.com/arts-culture/behind-the-gory-scenes-of-splatter-theater/
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: 'wearable gizmos modified to allow performers to disgorge blood on cue' in a stage splatter show. Other results concerned prosthetic makeup in films (The Substance, X) that are not clearly splatter.
genres.uncertainty: The definition centres on special effects, not the actor. The source is about a stage parody. Wearing blood rigs is not heavy character transformation, so no transformation tag was given.

genres.claim: Sports films ask actors to train in the sport depicted so they read as believable athletes.
genres.source: NPR, 'How actors in The Boys in the Boat trained to appear believable as Olympic athletes', https://www.npr.org/2023/12/20/1220558981/how-actors-in-the-boys-in-the-boat-trained-to-appear-believable-as-olympic-athle ; The Hollywood Reporter, 'Grading 15 Actors' Sports Skills in Movies', https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/grading-actors-sports-skills-movies/
genres.sourceSupports: NPR headline and snippet: the actors trained to row like the 1936 U.S. Olympic crew in order to 'appear believable as Olympic athletes'. THR grades actors on the sports skill they display on screen.

tags.why: The sources show sustained athletic physical action trained for the role, which the vocabulary's 'sustained physical action' covers.

genres.uncertainty: The NPR page timed out on fetch; headline and snippet only. 'stunt' maps to Stage Combat, which fits combat sports (boxing films) better than rowing or baseball; the fit is partial.

genres.claim: No source found that establishes cover-identity playing or stunt work as a convention of the spy genre for actors.
genres.source: Deadline, 'Keri Russell Is The Russian Next Door In The Americans', https://deadline.com/2014/06/the-offer-to-play-a-russian-spy-came-in-from-the-cold-for-keri-russell-791418/
genres.sourceSupports: Russell says (snippet) she did not focus much on 'the spy stuff' in building Elizabeth Jennings and was more interested in the marriage; she compares the double life to the 'whole other life' every person has.
genres.uncertainty: The one actor source found plays down the spy-specific demand. Accent was not sourced even though the role is a Russian posing as an American. Action-led spy films likely involve stunts, but no source was found.

genres.claim: No source found on what steampunk asks of actors. Sources describe Victorian-styled costume only.
genres.source: Creepy Catalog, '25+ Steampunk Movies', https://creepycatalog.com/steampunk-movies/
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: characters typically wear Victorian-era top hats, corsets, petticoats and trench coats.
genres.uncertainty: Costume is a design convention, not an acting demand. Period speech was not sourced for steampunk.

genres.claim: Stoner comedy is a comedy subgenre; its founding duo, Cheech and Chong, worked largely from improvisation.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Cheech & Chong', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheech_&_Chong (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: 'Much of their live act and albums featured improvised dialogue'; Up in Smoke reportedly worked from a yellow legal pad with a 'loose roadmap'.

tags.why: The genre is defined as a subgenre of comedy; the tag follows from the definition, not from an acting source.

genres.uncertainty: Improvisation is documented for one duo only, not as a convention of the genre, so no improvisation tag. Wikipedia is a pointer.

genres.claim: Superhero roles ask for intensive physical training and learned fight choreography.
genres.source: Deseret News, 'Superhero stunts demand a blend of fighting styles', https://www.deseret.com/2012/5/1/20410141/superhero-stunts-demand-a-blend-of-fighting-styles/ ; InsideHook, 'The Fitness Regimens 7 Actors Used to Get Into Superhero Shape', https://www.insidehook.com/wellness/how-to-get-into-superhero-shape
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: actors spent months learning the body mechanics of martial arts before fight sequences were built around them; Johansson describes choreographed steps 'to make it safe'; Larson's training combined lifting with fight-choreography sessions.

tags.why: Sources describe months of fight training and choreographed fights as the preparation the roles demanded.

genres.uncertainty: Snippets only. Green-screen work, also likely, has no vocabulary tag and was not sourced here.

genres.claim: No source found that establishes an acting demand specific to supernatural films.
genres.source: The Hollywood Reporter, 'Ghostbusters: How the Visual Effects Team Brought Slimer...', https://hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/ghostbusters-how-visual-effects-team-911727/amp
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: the production used actresses on set as ghosts so the cast could react to them rather than to a tennis ball.
genres.uncertainty: One production and an effects article. Reacting to unseen presences has no vocabulary tag.

genres.claim: Buñuel, the defining surrealist filmmaker, told actors as little as possible and directed them mostly through physical movement and outward gesture.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Filmmaking technique of Luis Buñuel', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmmaking_technique_of_Luis_Bu%C3%B1uel (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: 'Buñuel told actors as little as possible, and limited his directions mostly to physical movements'; another result notes control of actors 'with special attention paid to gesture and outward appearance'.
genres.uncertainty: One director stands for the movement. The source supports a non-psychological approach but no vocabulary tag.

genres.claim: Survival films can rest on a single actor with almost no dialogue; All Is Lost has one actor and about 51 words.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'All Is Lost', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Is_Lost (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: no other actors in the film and very few lines of dialogue (51 words). A review site describes DiCaprio in The Revenant conveying pain 'through grunts, moans, and sheer bodily exertion'.
genres.uncertainty: Two films stand for the genre. Physical endurance is implied but no credible source documents it as an actor demand. The physical-survival definition does not on its own entail stunt work, so no stunt tag.

genres.claim: Italian pepla cast bodybuilders, led by Steve Reeves, as their heroes.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Steve Reeves', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Reeves (pointer); The Film Magazine, 'A Journey Into Italian Peplum (c.1958-1965)', https://www.thefilmagazine.com/italian-peplum-c-1958-1965/
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: Reeves, a former Mr. Universe, made 14 pepla from 1957 to 1964, and many bodybuilders followed him to Italy to play Herculean leads.
genres.uncertainty: Sources support a casting convention (physique), which has no vocabulary tag. Sword combat and declamatory delivery were not sourced.

genres.claim: The genre's defining film had its lead train in heavy broadsword fighting, falls and riding.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Conan the Barbarian (1982 film)', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_the_Barbarian_(1982_film) (pointer); Yardbarker, 'Arnold Schwarzenegger Recalls Hours of Training With a Japanese Swordsman', https://www.yardbarker.com/general_sports/articles/arnold_schwarzenegger_recalls_hours_of_training_with_a_japanese_swordsman_to_perfect_conan_the_barbarian/s1_17782_43964330
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: Schwarzenegger trained with an 11-pound broadsword two hours a day for three months under swordmaster Kiyoshi Yamazaki, plus weapons, martial-arts and riding training, and learned to fall, roll and jump from fifteen feet.

tags.why: Months of sword training and falls for the genre's touchstone film; the definition itself centres on sword-wielding heroes in violent adventures.

genres.uncertainty: One film. Heightened mythic delivery was not sourced.

genres.claim: No source found on delivering technical jargon. One techno-thriller series had its cast attend hacking seminars and its lead learn to type code on camera.
genres.source: Engadget, 'Mr. Robot has an FBI consultant to make hacking look authentic', https://www.engadget.com/2016-03-14-mr-robot-sxsw-interview.html
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: the cast and creator attended hacking seminars; Malek had a typing instructor and typed parts of real code as the camera rolled.
genres.uncertainty: One series; technical credibility has no vocabulary tag.

genres.claim: Teen films and series often cast actors in their twenties or older as high-school characters.
genres.source: IndieWire, 'Adult Actors Playing Teenagers', https://www.indiewire.com/gallery/adult-actors-playing-teenagers/ ; TV Tropes, 'Dawson Casting' (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets list examples (Grease, Clueless, Dawson's Creek, Gossip Girl) of adults playing teenagers.
genres.uncertainty: This is a casting convention, not a skill demand, and has no vocabulary tag. Nothing found on adolescent behaviour as a skill.

genres.claim: No source found on thriller acting. Sources describe tension built by editing, close-ups, silence and pacing.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Thriller film', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller_film (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: tension 'is created by delaying what the audience sees as inevitable' through menacing situations. Nothing on performance.
genres.uncertainty: No acting source. Restraint under pressure is a reasonable reading but is unsourced.

genres.claim: In Looper, playing a younger version of another actor's character took daily prosthetics and close study of the older actor's mannerisms and voice.
genres.source: Screen Rant, 'How Looper Made Joseph Gordon-Levitt Look (& Sound) Like Bruce Willis', https://screenrant.com/looper-joseph-gordon-levitt-bruce-willis-face-effects/ ; The Hollywood Reporter, 'Looper: Joseph Gordon-Levitt Talks Physical Transformation', https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/dark-knight-joseph-gordon-levitt-looper-rian-johnson-bruce-willis-311133/
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: a 3-hour daily prosthetic process (nose, lip pieces, eyebrows, contacts); Gordon-Levitt studied Willis's performances and Willis recorded some lines for him to hear.

tags.why: Daily prosthetic makeup and studied mannerisms to become another actor's character, as documented for Looper.

genres.uncertainty: One film; playing two versions of a character is not established as a genre convention.

genres.claim: Classical tragedy is enacted in language 'enriched with ornaments' (Aristotle); Greek tragic actors wore masks and the choral parts were sung.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Tragedy', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy (pointer, quoting Aristotle's Poetics); Almeida Theatre, 'Greek Theatre: At A Glance', https://almeida.co.uk/get-involved/resource-hub/greek-theatre-at-a-glance/
genres.sourceSupports: Wikipedia: Aristotle defines tragedy as enacted 'by means of language enriched [with ornaments]'; 'All actors were male and wore masks'; choral parts were sung. Almeida: masks 'allowing actors to play multiple roles' with exaggerated features read from a distance; tragic actors wore raised boots.

tags.why: Aristotle's definition makes ornamented, heightened language part of what tragedy is.
Almeida and Wikipedia both state that Greek tragic actors performed in masks, often playing several roles.

genres.uncertainty: Both tags hold for classical (Greek and verse) tragedy, not for modern prose or film tragedy. Almeida's page did not mention verse when read; that came from Wikipedia's account of Aristotle.

genres.claim: Dramatised true crime means playing real people, which coaches treat as research into the person's voice, accent and mannerisms.
genres.source: StageMilk, 'Playing a Real-Life Person as an Actor', https://www.stagemilk.com/playing-a-real-life-person-as-an-actor/
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: 'A lot of actors will jump straight to accent, and that is an important part of the process!'; if the person was recorded, watch to see how they spoke and presented themselves; study physical mannerisms.

tags.why: StageMilk names accent as an important part of preparing to play a real person, which dramatised true crime always involves.

genres.uncertainty: The source is about playing real people generally, not true crime specifically. The accent tag only applies when the real person's speech differs from the actor's.

genres.claim: Actors in vampire roles may have to learn to speak clearly in prosthetic fangs; several notable Draculas wore none.
genres.source: TV Tropes, 'Fang Thpeak', https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FangThpeak (pointer only)
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: prosthetic fangs make some sounds hard to pronounce; Juliet Landau wore hers for a long period before playing Drusilla to learn to speak with them; Langella and Lugosi wore no fangs as Dracula.
genres.uncertainty: TV Tropes is not credible enough to carry a tag. The Stan Winston School page on Interview with the Vampire returned no text on fetch. Fang work is minor prosthetics, not heavy transformation.

genres.claim: War films routinely put casts through military boot camps run by advisers so they can play soldiers credibly.
genres.source: Military.com, 'Meet the Man Who Puts Movie Stars Through Boot Camp', https://www.military.com/podcasts/left-of-boom/2021/02/16/dale-dyes-movie-stars-boot-camp.html ; Coffee or Die, 'These Acclaimed War Movies Took Realistic Preparation to Extreme Levels', https://www.coffeeordie.com/article/platoon-movie-boot-camps
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: Dale Dye ran a 30-day military-style boot camp for the Platoon cast and an intensive one for Saving Private Ryan (sleeping in rain, 5-mile runs); his company Warriors Inc. trains actors for war films.

tags.why: Sources document sustained military physical training for combat roles as standard preparation.

genres.uncertainty: Military drill and bearing have no exact vocabulary tag; 'stunt' covers the physical-action part only. Snippets.

genres.claim: Western productions run 'cowboy camps' that teach actors horse riding and gun handling.
genres.source: CinemaBlend, 'I Thought Yellowstone's Cowboy Camp Was About Learning To Rope And Ride...', https://www.cinemablend.com/interviews/i-thought-yellowstone-cowboy-camp-learning-rope-ride-marshals-star-schooled-me-what-actors-really-need-know ; Netflix Tudum, 'Ransom Canyon cast cowboy boot camp', https://www.netflix.com/tudum/videos/ransom-canyon-behind-the-scenes-cowboy-boot-camp
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: camps teach riding, mounting and dismounting, roping and firearm handling; Tim Blake Nelson trained with guns for about five months for gun tricks in The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.

tags.why: Riding and gun handling are trained physical-action skills the sources show westerns requiring; firearms handling falls within stage-combat training.

genres.uncertainty: The examples are mostly recent TV westerns. Horsemanship is not stage combat, so the stunt tag fits only part. Laconic manner was not sourced.

genres.claim: For Murder on the Orient Express (2017), Branagh studied Belgian accents with a dialect coach three times a week to play Poirot.

genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: Branagh listened to recordings of 27 Belgian accents and met a dialect coach three times a week to practise Poirot's accent.

tags.why: The source documents dialect coaching for the detective in a canonical whodunit.

genres.uncertainty: One production and one role. The accent belongs to Poirot, not to the whodunit form. Ensemble suspect-playing was not sourced.

genres.claim: Ninkyo (chivalry) yakuza films built their stars on stoic, sword-carrying honour; Fukasaku's 1970s jitsuroku films replaced this with rougher, more realistic fights.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Ken Takakura', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Takakura (pointer); Wikipedia, 'Kinji Fukasaku', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinji_Fukasaku (pointer); BFI, '10 great Japanese gangster films', https://www.bfi.org.uk/lists/10-great-japanese-gangster-films
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: Takakura appeared as 'stoic, tattooed, katana-wielding tough guys' with a brooding, strong-but-silent style; Fukasaku's films were 'rough and violent with more realistic fights'.

tags.why: Both cycles as described involve fight action, sword-fighting in ninkyo and realistic brawls in jitsuroku.

genres.uncertainty: The sources describe screen personas and film style, not what actors trained for. The stunt tag is inferred from described fight content, which makes it weak.

genres.claim: The action genre is defined by fights, chases, shootouts and stunt work.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Action film', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_film (pointer)

genres.uncertainty: Wikipedia is a pointer. Stunt work is often done by doubles, so the page does not say the actor does it.

genres.claim: Action comedy combines action with humour that plays a central role, descended from silent comedians' chases, gags and stunts.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Action comedy', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_comedy (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: Read via a summarising fetch: humour 'plays a relatively central role'; silent comedians such as Chaplin and Keaton featured 'chases, gags and stunts'. The earlier quoted phrase 'relies on the characters to bring out the humor' did not come back in this read.

tags.why: The genre is action plus comedy; the page links its roots to chases and stunts.
Humour 'plays a relatively central role' by definition.

genres.uncertainty: The fetch tool summarised the page; its remarks on Jackie Chan may be the summariser's gloss, so no physicalComedy tag was given.

genres.claim: In a backstage musical the story stops for diegetic performance numbers in a show being produced.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Backstage musical', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backstage_musical (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'The film's narrative trajectory often comes to a halt one or more times to allow a performance'; the songs are 'diegetic numbers'; plots revolve around 'the production of a play or musical revue'; Busby Berkeley typified the genre.

tags.why: Performance numbers with songs are the genre's defining feature.
The plots stage musical revues and the genre is typified by Busby Berkeley's production numbers.

genres.uncertainty: The page names 'songs' and 'performances' explicitly; dance follows from 'musical revue' and Berkeley rather than from an explicit sentence about dancing.

genres.claim: Comic timing, the use of pauses, cadence, delivery and pacing to land a joke, is the core comic skill.
genres.source: MasterClass, 'Guide to Comedic Timing', https://www.masterclass.com/articles/guide-to-comedic-timing
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: 'Comedic timing is the use of pauses, cadence, delivery, and pacing to land a joke.'

tags.why: The source defines comic timing as the craft comedy rests on.

genres.uncertainty: MasterClass returned HTTP 403 on fetch; the definition came back in search. The 'listening to scene partners' part of the earlier claim was not re-confirmed.

genres.claim: Docufiction's main characters are often non-professionals essentially playing themselves, unscripted, with improvised dialogue and genuine reactions.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Docufiction', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Docufiction (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'The main character or characters—often portrayed by non-professional or amateur actors—are essentially playing themselves'; docufictions 'are usually not scripted' and use participants' 'own genuine reactions and their own improvisational dialogue'.

tags.why: The page says docufictions are usually unscripted, with improvisational dialogue.
Participants portray 'their own genuine reactions' on camera, which is naturalistic on-camera behaviour as a convention.

genres.uncertainty: The participants are often not actors at all, so 'demand on an actor' applies loosely.

genres.claim: Farce calls for highly stylised performances and dramatic reactions, with adept comic timing for wordplay, visual gags and slapstick.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Farce', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farce (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'broad, larger-than-life characters, often calling for highly stylized performances and dramatic reactions'; 'There may be wordplay, visual gags and slapstick, requiring the need for adept comic timing by the actors.'

tags.why: 'requiring the need for adept comic timing by the actors'.
Visual gags and slapstick are named conventions of the form.

genres.uncertainty: 'Highly stylized performances' is about physical and emotional style, not language, so no heightened tag.

genres.claim: Found-footage films routinely use improvisation and naturalistic acting, and the actors may shoot the film themselves as they perform.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Found footage (film technique)', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Found_footage_(film_technique) (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'the cinematography may be done by the actors themselves as they perform'; 'shaky camera work, improvisation and naturalistic acting are routinely employed'.

tags.why: 'improvisation ... routinely employed'.
'naturalistic acting' is routine, and actors may operate the camera.

genres.uncertainty: Wikipedia is a pointer.

genres.claim: Jidaigeki uses a contrived, formal, archaic register of Japanese speech, stock makeup and catchphrases, and stylised sword fights.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Jidaigeki', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jidaigeki (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'A contrived form of old-fashioned Japanese speech, using modern pronunciation and grammar with a high degree of formality and frequent archaisms'; heroes wear eye makeup; protagonists deliver set catchphrases (kimarizerifu); sword fights follow set conventions, and chambara films use stylised violence.

tags.why: The page describes a formal, archaic stylised speech register as a convention.
Sword fights are a standing convention; chambara is the sword-fighting branch.

genres.uncertainty: Read through a summarising fetch. The page does not say how much of the swordplay the lead actors do themselves.

genres.claim: Japanese kaiju films used suit actors performing inside stiff latex or rubber creature suits on miniature sets.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Kaiju', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaiju (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: Tsuburaya 'decided to attempt to create suits, called creature suits, for a human (suit actor) to wear and act in'; 'Due to the extreme stiffness of the latex or rubber suits, filming would often be done at double speed'; combined with miniature city sets.

tags.why: Suit actors perform as the creature inside full creature suits.

genres.uncertainty: The tag fits suit actors, not the human cast. Reacting to unseen threats was not sourced on this read.

genres.claim: Martial-arts roles are often played by real martial artists; otherwise actors train for the role, helped by doubles, wire work and camera tricks.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Martial arts film', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_arts_film (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'these roles are often played by actors who are real martial artists. If not, actors frequently train in preparation for their roles or the action director may rely more on stylized action or film making tricks'; techniques include 'doubles, undercranking, wire work'.

tags.why: Real martial-arts skill or role-specific fight training is stated as the norm.

genres.uncertainty: Wikipedia is a pointer.

genres.claim: Film melodrama uses exaggerated staging, score and performance; characters wear their hearts on their sleeves.
genres.source: BFI, 'Too Much: Melodrama on Film', https://www.bfi.org.uk/too-much
genres.sourceSupports: Melodrama 'employs exaggerated staging, score and performance to create the ultimate spectacle'; 'a passionate purge of emotion'; 'heightened dramatics'; characters 'rarely behave rationally'.
genres.uncertainty: The source supports exaggerated emotional performance, but the vocabulary's 'heightened' tag means heightened or stylised language, which the BFI does not mention. No tag fits, and none was forced.

genres.claim: Mockumentaries can be partly or wholly improvised and are presented through documentary devices such as talking heads and cinéma vérité.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Mockumentary', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mockumentary (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'Mockumentaries can be partly or wholly improvised'; 'often presented as historical documentaries, with B roll and talking heads ... or as cinéma vérité pieces'.

tags.why: The page states mockumentaries can be partly or wholly improvised.

genres.uncertainty: Deadpan naturalism was not explicitly stated, so no camera tag. The page did not establish that mockumentaries are always comic, so no comic tag.

genres.claim: Naturalism in performance and dialogue is a key feature of almost all mumblecore; early films used non-professionals and some used prominent improvisation.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Mumblecore', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumblecore (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'Naturalism – both in performance and dialogue – is a key feature of almost all mumblecore films'; 'Early mumblecore films tended to feature non-professional actors'; 'Some mumblecore films feature a prominent use of improvisation, with the cast sharing script credits'; Bujalski's are 'mostly scripted'.

tags.why: Naturalistic performance is called a key feature of almost all mumblecore films.
Some films feature prominent improvisation, with the cast sharing script credits.

genres.uncertainty: Improvisation is 'some' films, not all; the page notes mostly scripted exceptions.

genres.claim: A musical film integrates musical numbers into the plot; characters sing and dance.
genres.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Musical film', https://www.britannica.com/art/musical-film
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: a musical film 'integrates musical numbers within the plot'; characters often sing and dance to express emotion and advance the plot.

tags.why: Britannica: musical numbers integrated in the plot; characters sing.
Britannica (snippet): characters sing and dance.

genres.uncertainty: Britannica pages return HTTP 403 to fetch; the search summary may blend Britannica with other results, especially the sing-and-dance sentence.

genres.claim: Nature documentaries almost all have a human presenter, whose role ranges from explanatory voice-over to on-camera interaction with animals.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Nature documentary', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_documentary (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'Almost all have a human presenter, the role varies widely, ranging from explanatory voice-overs to extensive interaction or even confrontation with animals.'

tags.why: Explanatory voice-over is named as a standard presenter role.

genres.uncertainty: Presenting is not acting in the usual sense; on-camera presenting has no exact tag.

genres.claim: Italian neorealism was filmed on location among the poor and working class, frequently with non-professional actors.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Italian neorealism', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_neorealism (pointer); previously cited: Britannica, 'Neorealism', https://www.britannica.com/art/Neorealism-Italian-art (not reachable)
genres.sourceSupports: Wikipedia snippet: 'a style of film characterized by stories set amongst the poor and working class, filmed on location, frequently using nonprofessional actors'; where known actors were cast they played 'strongly against their normal character types'.

tags.why: Non-professionals playing ordinary people on location is the movement's defining convention, which implies unadorned on-camera naturalism.

genres.uncertainty: The Britannica page could not be read (403), and searches returned Wikipedia and others instead. The camera tag is inferred from casting and location practice; no source here states a performance style in so many words.

genres.claim: The New Wave promoted a naturalistic style with location shooting, improvised dialogue and natural light.
genres.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'New Wave', https://www.britannica.com/art/New-Wave-film
genres.sourceSupports: Search summary attributed to Britannica: 'The New Wave movement promoted a more naturalistic filmmaking style, with location shoots, improvised dialogue, and natural lighting.'

tags.why: Improvised dialogue is named as a convention.
The movement is described as promoting a naturalistic style.

genres.uncertainty: The Britannica page could not be fetched, and the search did not return the New Wave page itself, so the attribution is unconfirmed. Treat as secondhand.

genres.claim: Period dramas employ historical advisers who teach actors how to speak, stand, sit, eat and gesture in the manner of the era.
genres.source: Detroit News, 'PBS special examines the etiquette of Downton Abbey', https://eu.detroitnews.com/story/entertainment/television/2015/01/04/downton-abbey-pbs-special/21210235/ ; PBS, 'The Manners of Downton Abbey', https://cm-pressroom.pbs.org/programs/m/manners-of-downton-abbey ; previously cited: DataCalculus, 'Dialect coaching for actors in period pieces'
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: Alastair Bruce advised Downton Abbey actors 'on how to speak, stand, sit, eat, drink, dress', posture and 'the use of vocabulary'; Lily James: 'The main thing I had to learn was posture'. DataCalculus (read) says dialect coaches evoke 'the culture, education, and social class of the period'.

tags.why: The Downton sources document coaching in period speech, vocabulary and manners as part of the work.

genres.uncertainty: The earlier source, DataCalculus, is a data-analytics company's blog and too weak to carry a tag, so no accent tag was given. The Downton evidence is one series.

genres.claim: Under the Hays Code, romantic comedies relied on verbal sparring and physical comedy.
genres.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Romantic comedy', https://www.britannica.com/art/romantic-comedy-film
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: the Hays Code 'prohibited explicit mention of sexual relationships, leading to films' relying on verbal sparring and physical comedy instead'; the genre is defined by the lighthearted pursuit of love.

tags.why: The genre is comedy, and Britannica names verbal sparring as a defining resource.

genres.uncertainty: Britannica could not be fetched (403). Physical comedy is tied to the Hays-era films, so no physicalComedy tag for the genre as a whole. Chemistry has no tag.

genres.claim: Samurai films use tate, a stage swordplay of fixed forms that actors memorise and combine, with strict posture and etiquette.
genres.source: The Gate (thegate12.com), article on tate, https://thegate12.com/article/283
genres.sourceSupports: Tate is 'stage fighting in brawls or with swords, in stage plays and movies' using fixed forms actors memorise and combine; it requires straight back and planted heels, proper kimono wear and sword etiquette.

tags.why: The page describes learned, choreographed stage swordplay for film and stage.

genres.uncertainty: The Gate is a Japan-culture travel site describing a tate experience, not an academic source. Period bearing has no exact tag.

genres.claim: Screwball comedy is built on fast-paced, overlapping repartee combined with slapstick.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Screwball comedy', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screwball_comedy (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'fast-paced, overlapping repartee'; 'slapstick elements'; Henry Fonda performs 'numerous pratfalls' in The Lady Eve.

tags.why: Fast, overlapping verbal repartee is the genre's defining feature.
Slapstick elements and pratfalls are named.

genres.uncertainty: Read through a summarising fetch.

genres.sourceSupports: The page discusses 'nautical language' and 'the vernacular expression of seafaring men' in fiction such as Cooper's The Pilot. It says nothing about film actors or physical work in water.

genres.claim: Silent-film actors conveyed story and emotion through mime, pantomime and exaggerated gesture and expression.
genres.source: StudioBinder, 'What is a Silent Film', https://www.studiobinder.com/blog/what-is-a-silent-film-definition/
genres.sourceSupports: 'Actors in silent films often used techniques of mime and pantomime to convey emotions and actions, making performances highly expressive and physical'; 'exaggerated expressions and gestures'.
genres.uncertainty: No tag in the fixed vocabulary fits wordless pantomime: physicalComedy means slapstick and clowning, and silent drama is not comic. A vocabulary gap, not a lack of evidence. StudioBinder is a production-software blog.

genres.claim: Ken Loach, the touchstone of British social realism, casts non-professionals alongside actors, withholds the full script, shoots in sequence and encourages improvisation.
genres.source: No Film School, 'Ten Directing Lessons Inspired by Ken Loach', https://nofilmschool.com/directed-by-ken-loach ; Into Film, 'Ken Loach, social realism...', https://www.intofilm.org/news-and-views/articles/ken-loach-feature
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: Loach uses non-professionals, limits actors' access to the script, shoots chronologically, 'avoids extensive rehearsals and encourages actors to improvise as a way of achieving spontaneity'.

tags.why: Loach encourages actors to improvise for spontaneity.
The method aims at spontaneous, naturalistic on-camera behaviour.

genres.uncertainty: The Into Film page returned no text when fetched. One director's method stands for the genre.

genres.claim: Fight directors such as Paddy Crean staged swashbuckler swordplay and taught actors sword work for stage and film.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Paddy Crean', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Crean (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: Crean ran a London fencing school 'used ... to teach many celebrities sword work for stage and films', often doubled for Errol Flynn, and choreographed films such as The Master of Ballantrae (1953).

tags.why: Staged swordplay taught by a fight director is documented for the genre's films.

genres.uncertainty: Crean often doubled Flynn, so some swordplay was not performed by the star.

genres.claim: Tokusatsu suit actors do their stunts and sword fights inside full costumes that hide their faces, acting through body language, with voices dubbed later.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Suit actor', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suit_actor (pointer)
genres.sourceSupports: 'the suit actor does all of their stunts while in a full costume that normally obscures their identity'; roles 'may require extensive sword fights, actions and stunts within a physically restrictive environment'; 'extensive body language and pantomime are crucial'; 'the actor's voice is dubbed during after-recording'.

tags.why: Suit actors do stunts and sword fights in costume.
Full-costume performance with the face hidden, conveyed through body language.

genres.uncertainty: Applies to suit actors, not the unmasked cast. Voice dubbing is done to the suit actor, not by them, so no voiceWork tag.

genres.claim: Tragicomedy holds tragic and comic elements side by side, with tone shifting between serious and comic, often within a scene.
genres.source: StudioBinder, 'What is Tragicomedy', https://www.studiobinder.com/blog/what-is-tragicomedy-definition/ ; Fiveable, 'Tragicomedy', https://fiveable.me/english-12/key-terms/tragicomedy
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: tragicomedies 'hold comedy and tragedy side by side in balance'; the tone 'shifts between serious and comic, often within the same scene'. A Semantic Scholar paper notes Chekhov asked the Moscow Art Theatre for 'a lighter touch'.

tags.why: By definition the form contains comedy the actor must play alongside tragic stakes.

genres.uncertainty: These are genre guides, not acting sources. The tag comes from the definition.

genres.claim: Werewolf roles can require long prosthetic transformations that the actor must perform through.
genres.source: The Hollywood Reporter, 'Wolf Man Star Christopher Abbott Talks His 7-Hour Transformation', https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-features/wolf-man-star-christopher-abbott-1236109770/ ; IndieWire, 'Wolf Man: Christopher Abbott Needed 650 Prosthetic Pieces', https://www.indiewire.com/features/craft/wolf-man-christopher-abbott-650-prosthetic-pieces-interview-1235085626/
genres.sourceSupports: Snippets: the final transformation stage took up to seven hours; Abbott called it 'tedious and arduous' and practised lines in a mirror to see 'how your face moves underneath the prosthetics'.

tags.why: Heavy multi-stage prosthetic transformation the actor performs through.

genres.uncertainty: One film; earlier werewolf films vary (some used CGI).

genres.claim: Wuxia films by King Hu and the Shaw Brothers used wire- and trampoline-assisted acrobatics and choreographed sword action.
genres.source: Wikipedia, 'Wuxia', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuxia (pointer); Wikipedia, 'Wire fu' (snippet only)
genres.sourceSupports: 'sophisticated action choreography using wire and trampoline assisted acrobatics combined with sped-up camera techniques'; Yuen Woo-ping became famous as a wuxia action choreographer.

tags.why: Choreographed, wire-assisted acrobatic fight action is a defining convention.

genres.uncertainty: The page does not say how much the actors perform themselves rather than doubles.

genres.claim: Zombie productions train performers to move consistently as the undead, taught by the stunt team.
genres.source: TheWrap, 'Army of the Dead: Zack Snyder Sent Hundreds of Extras to Zombie School', https://www.thewrap.com/army-of-the-dead-zack-snyder-extras-zombie-school/
genres.sourceSupports: Snippet: about 200 extras attended 'Zombie School', where the stunt team taught them 'how to move and act like a zombie'. Walking Dead extras also attended a zombie school (Collider).

tags.why: Trained creature movement for undead roles, under makeup.

genres.uncertainty: Applies to undead performers (largely extras), not the living leads. Survival physicality for the living cast was not sourced.
